standard.title: Texts organised by purpose
standard.description: identify how texts across the curriculum are organised differently and use language features depending on purposes
standard.prior_knowledge: Students explore how texts are organised differently according to their purpose (AC9E1LA03). They have not yet identified specific structural and language features associated with distinct text types across curriculum areas, or recognised that the same purpose can be expressed in different forms.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify how texts across the curriculum are organised differently and use specific language features depending on their purposes.

nodes.label: Purpose drives organisation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the purpose of a text and connect that purpose to at least one organisational feature.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the purpose of a familiar text type (e.g. narrative, procedure) and name one organisational feature that serves that purpose.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and compare the purposes of several text types and connect each purpose to its typical organisational features across narrative, recount, information report and procedure.
wider: Compare two texts with the same purpose but different organisations (e.g. a procedure as a list vs as a video) and discuss how the form affects the audience
Explore informative texts from Science or HASS and identify how their purpose shapes their organisation

response_modes.reason: Students often think organisational features are arbitrary rules rather than purposeful choices. Seeing the same purpose realised in different text types, and different purposes in similar formats, resolves the misconception that structure is fixed. Multiple text type examples across curriculum areas are the productive move.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-curriculum examples are a genuinely rich direction — every subject area produces texts with distinctive organisations (science reports, maths word problems, HASS recounts) and each new example deepens understanding of how purpose drives organisation.
success_criteria: Student can name the purpose of a given text and identify at least one organisational feature that serves that purpose.
Student does not claim that all texts of the same type are organised identically — they can acknowledge variation.

nodes.label: Language features signal text type
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify language features — such as time connectives in recounts, imperative verbs in procedures, technical vocabulary in reports — that signal a text's type and purpose.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one language feature in a text that signals its purpose (e.g. imperative verbs in a procedure, past tense in a recount).
nodes.typical_width: Identify and name language features in narratives, recounts, information reports, simple procedures, opinions and responses to texts, and explain how each feature supports the text's purpose.
wider: Compare how the same topic is presented in a narrative and an information report, identifying the different language features each uses
Identify language features in poetry that differ from prose text types and discuss how they serve poetic purposes
success_criteria: Student can name a language feature in a text and explain how it supports the text's purpose.
Student can distinguish language features across at least two different text types.

nodes.label: Same purpose, different forms
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that a single purpose (e.g. expressing an opinion) can be expressed through different text forms — poster, email, brochure — and that the form shapes the language features used.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two different forms that serve the same purpose and name one way the language or organisation differs between them.
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how opinion, information or recount purposes can each be realised across multiple forms, and identify how the chosen form shapes language features, layout and audience expectations.
wider: Create or compare two versions of the same message in different forms (e.g. a recount as a letter and as a multimodal presentation) and discuss how the form changes the language
Identify texts in digital formats (website, infographic, ebook) and compare their organisation to print equivalents

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the two prior understandings — purpose drives organisation AND language features signal text type — and adds the insight that form is a third variable. Coordinating all three is the learning challenge here.

success_criteria: Student can identify that the same purpose can take different forms.
Student can name at least one way language features or organisation changes when the form changes, even if the purpose stays the same.
